findings.claim: should_encode's own docstring says a column is encoded "if it holds text or choice values" but the actual set literal it checks against also includes "masked_text" -- a third kind the module-level docstring names as one of the four column kinds this library supports. The function's stated contract and its implementation disagree, and test_columnstore.py's fixture never constructs a masked_text column (plain or Packed), so nothing exercises the kind the docstring omits.
findings.source: columnstore.py:60-64 `"""A column should be one-hot encoded if it holds text or choice\n    values..."""` followed by `return kind in {"text", "masked_text", "choice"}`; test_columnstore.py:17-26 `_table()` fixture (no masked_text column, plain or Packed)
findings.remedy: Update should_encode's docstring to name masked_text explicitly, and add a masked_text column (and a Packed("masked_text") column) to the test fixture so the claim is verified rather than only asserted.

findings.claim: The Packed-unwrap rule ("use col.kind.primitive when kind is a Packed, otherwise col.kind itself") is written out identically in both column_subset and should_encode. Nothing about either function requires it to differ from the other; if a second wrapper type or unwrap rule is added, it is easy to update one call site and miss the other.
findings.source: columnstore.py:53 `alias = col.kind.primitive if isinstance(col.kind, Packed) else col.kind` and columnstore.py:63 `kind = col.kind.primitive if isinstance(col.kind, Packed) else col.kind`
findings.remedy: Extract a one-line helper, e.g. `_primitive_kind(col: Column) -> str`, and call it from both column_subset and should_encode. Same behavior for every existing caller of either function.

findings.claim: fieldspec.py's docstring says an annotation "may also be wrapped in Tagged[...]" AND separately "may arrive as an unresolved forward reference", implying the two can combine (a Tagged-wrapped annotation that itself fails to eval). _DERIVED_PATTERN's structure (`((\w+\.)?Tagged\[)?(\w+\.)?Derived\[`) does account for an optional leading "Tagged[" before "Derived[", so the combined case is handled -- but no test in test_fieldspec.py ever passes a source string like `'Tagged[Derived[Missing], "x"]'`. The existing Tagged test (test_tagged_wrapped_derived_field_is_excluded) uses a fully-resolvable namespace, so it never reaches the regex fallback at all, and the existing unresolved-forward-ref test (test_bare_forward_ref_derived_field_is_excluded) isn't Tagged-wrapped. The one code path that combines both disclosed edge cases has zero coverage.
findings.source: fieldspec.py:7-10 docstring ("may also be wrapped in `Tagged[...]`" / "unresolved forward reference"); fieldspec.py:24 `_DERIVED_PATTERN = re.compile(r"((\w+\.)?Tagged\[)?(\w+\.)?Derived\[")`; test_fieldspec.py:37-46 (Tagged case is resolvable, forward-ref case is not Tagged-wrapped)
findings.remedy: Add `stored_field_names({"total": "int", "cached_total": 'Tagged[Derived[Missing], "x"]'}, NAMESPACE)` asserting `["total"]`, to prove the Tagged+unresolved fallback the docstring describes actually works.

findings.claim: CHANGES.md describes Handle.span as changed from "a plain span: str attribute" to a read-only property, and certifies that "every existing caller that only ever read .span sees no change." That phrasing is scoped to readers; it does not say what happens to a caller that used to assign to .span. The property as written (`span` getter only, no setter) means any such assignment now raises AttributeError instead of updating the span, and test_lifespan.py exercises only reads (equality, dict-key, string formatting) -- never an assignment -- so this narrowing from read-write to read-only is not proven safe by anything shown here.
findings.source: lifespan.py:70-72 `@property\n    def span(self) -> str:\n        return self._span.value` (no setter defined); CHANGES.md:3-4 "`Handle` used to carry a plain `span: str` attribute... It now carries `_span: Span`... with a read-only `span` property" and CHANGES.md:9 "Every existing caller that only ever read `.span` sees no change"
findings.remedy: Either add a `span.setter` that resolves a string back to a Span via span_from_value (keeping .span read-write), or, if no caller anywhere ever assigns to .span, say that plainly instead of scoping the safety claim to readers only.

findings.claim: `actor QuietQueue {}` is declared but never referenced anywhere -- not in Workspace's initializers, not in child(at:), not in main.swift. The comment above it says as much ("not wired into any scoping path yet"). It is speculative scaffolding for a hypothetical future execution context, sitting in the same file as an otherwise complete, self-consistent generic store.
findings.source: workspace.swift:57-59 `// Reserved for a future default execution context; not wired into any\n// scoping path yet.\nactor QuietQueue {}`
findings.remedy: Delete QuietQueue and its comment. Nothing currently depends on it, so removing it changes nothing for any caller (deletion test passes trivially); add it back only when an actual scoping path needs a default execution context.

findings.claim: CHANGES.md's central claim is "No test's skip/run outcome changes on any platform" for merging three inline two-platform checks into is_driftplane. But test_platform_guards.py's main() only ever calls collect_skips against MAINLAND (asserting it skips nothing) and then runs every test body. It never calls collect_skips(GEARSHIFT, ALL_TESTS) or collect_skips(TIDELINE, ALL_TESTS) to confirm the three is_driftplane-guarded tests (test_shared_temp_writable, test_process_fork, test_large_page_alloc) still skip on both sandboxed platforms with their original reason text, or that the untouched single-platform and dual-guard tests are unaffected. The one claim this refactor most needs evidence for -- behavior on gearshift and tideline -- is exactly the claim this suite never runs.
findings.source: test_platform_guards.py:74-79 `def main() -> int:\n    skipped = collect_skips(MAINLAND, ALL_TESTS)\n    assert skipped == {}, ...` (no equivalent call for GEARSHIFT or TIDELINE); CHANGES.md:11 "No test's skip/run outcome changes on any platform."
findings.remedy: Add `collect_skips(GEARSHIFT, ALL_TESTS)` and `collect_skips(TIDELINE, ALL_TESTS)` assertions checking the expected skip set and reason strings for each, so the cross-platform preservation claim is executable evidence, not reasoning about mainland alone.
